opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a fair question to ask, and I understand where it comes from. NVIDIA is a computing company, and of course we sell GPUs. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But I'd frame it a little differently.

When we started working on Cosmos and the broader world foundation model effort, the motivation came from a very concrete problem: physical AI is bottlenecked by data. If you want to train a robot or an autonomous vehicle, you can't just scrape the internet the way you can for language. Collecting real-world data is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. You can't crash a thousand cars to learn what a crash looks like. So we asked, can we build models that understand how the world evolves, and use them to generate training data, evaluate policies, and let developers explore scenarios they could never safely capture in reality?

That's a research problem first. And the reason we released the models openly, with open weights, the tokenizers, the data curation pipeline, is that we believe no single company is going to solve physical AI alone. If we kept it closed and just used it internally, that would actually be a weaker story. By putting it out there, a robotics startup with a small team can fine-tune a world model for their own setup instead of spending years building one from scratch.

Now, does that create more demand for compute? Yes, probably. Training and running world models is computationally heavy. Video is heavy. But I'd say that's a consequence, not the purpose. It's similar to how better tools for deep learning a decade ago created more demand for GPUs. Nobody would say CUDA or cuDNN was "just a way to sell chips." They enabled a whole field to happen, and then the field grew.

And honestly, if the world models weren't useful, nobody would use them, and it wouldn't sell anything. The only way this strategy works is if the models genuinely help people build better robots and better self-driving systems. So the incentive is actually aligned: we have to make the technology good and make it accessible. That's what I care about as a researcher. I want to see physical AI actually work, robots in homes, in factories, helping people. If that happens and it also happens to be good for NVIDIA's business, I don't see a conflict there.

r001.rationale: The response says world models may increase compute demand, but frames that as a consequence of useful research. It does not argue that GPU investments should be judged by the profit they enable rather than the scale of GPU purchases.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a fair thing to ask, and I won't pretend NVIDIA isn't a company that sells GPUs. Of course we are. But I'd push back on the idea that that's what Cosmos or the world-model work is about.

Here's how I actually think about it. When we started on world foundation models, the problem we saw was very concrete: the people building robots and autonomous vehicles were stuck. They had plenty of compute. What they didn't have was data. You can scrape the internet to train a language model, but you can't scrape the internet to get a million examples of a robot arm failing to grasp a cup under bad lighting, or a car encountering a child running out between parked trucks at dusk. Those situations are rare, they're dangerous to collect, and they're expensive. So the bottleneck for physical AI was never "we need more GPUs." It was "we need a way to generate and reason about physical experience that we don't have."

A world model addresses that. It lets you take a small amount of real data and expand it into a much larger space of plausible scenarios. It lets a policy be evaluated against situations it has never seen. That's the actual motivation, and it's why we open-sourced the models and the tokenizers and the data pipeline. If the goal were simply to lock people into buying hardware, giving the weights away under a permissive license would be a strange strategy.

Now, is it true that if physical AI succeeds, people will buy more accelerators? Yes. I'm not going to be coy about that. But I'd say the causality runs the other direction from what the criticism implies. We're not inventing a use case to justify hardware. We're trying to solve a problem that researchers and companies have been telling us is blocking them, and if that creates demand, it's because the thing works.

The honest test is whether people who have no interest in buying anything from us still find the models useful. And I see that happening. Academic labs fine-tuning Cosmos on their own robots, startups using it for synthetic data on their own clusters, people running it on hardware we didn't make. That's the outcome I care about. If the ecosystem only mattered because of what it sold, it wouldn't survive contact with the research community, and so far it has.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether world-model work solves a real problem and may create accelerator demand, but it does not argue that GPU investments should be judged by the profit they enable rather than by GPU purchase scale.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a fair question. NVIDIA benefits when people use more compute, so we shouldn’t pretend there’s no business incentive. But the useful question is whether world models solve a problem that matters to developers.

For robotics, for example, collecting real-world experience can be expensive and slow. If a world model helps you generate useful training scenarios or test a system before deploying it, that can create value. But you have to demonstrate that the results transfer to the real world. Generating an impressive video isn’t enough.

So I would judge the ecosystem by outcomes: Does it help people build more capable systems? Does it reduce the time and total cost of development? If it does, selling GPUs and delivering value can go together. If it doesn’t, then the criticism is justified.

r001.rationale: The response says to judge the ecosystem by developer outcomes, capability, and development time and cost. It does not argue that GPU investments should be judged by the profit they enable rather than by GPU purchase scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a fair question. NVIDIA benefits when people use more compute, so there is a business incentive. But that alone doesn’t tell you whether the technology is useful.

The question I would focus on is: does a world model help you solve a problem better? Can you use it to generate useful training data, test a robot in difficult situations, or reduce the amount of real-world data you need? And can you measure that improvement against the cost of running the model?

If we’re just generating impressive videos and consuming GPUs, that criticism is justified. If we help developers build more capable systems with less time and expense, then there’s real value. We have to demonstrate that value, rather than ask people to accept the vision.

r001.rationale: The response says to judge world models by whether they solve problems and deliver value relative to operating cost, but it does not argue that GPU investments should be judged by the profit they enable.
